card.hook: Everyone has the same Eiffel Tower photo, and the secret is boringly simple: stand far enough back that the whole Iron Lady fits in one frame, toes to tip.
card.stand_here: Stand about 600 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From there you can see the four legs, the arches and the very top at once.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole tower in. Try 0.5x if you want lots of foreground or sky, and 3x to zoom in on the top section or the ironwork.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the ironwork looks dark and crisp.
card.best_time: Early morning is the quieter time, so you'll have fewer people wandering into your shot. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Trocadéro forecourt (Parvis des Droits-de-l'Homme) and face away from the tower so it sits behind you across the river, then use the front camera, or 0.5x if your phone has it, to get the landmark over your shoulder. It's crowded from mid-morning, so go early. For a different look, try Pont de Bir-Hakeim, where the bridge's ironwork frames you with the tower peeking out over the Seine.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at Place Joffre on the Champ de Mars, where the whole tower fits in the frame, while you pose with the tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Tickets are sold for going up the tower, so check the official site before you go. Selfie stick rules vary between guides and we found no official ruling, so check on arrival before you pull one out.
card.challenge: Line up one edge of the tower with a gridline, then wait for a stranger to stroll through the foreground so you get a photo with real scale.
card.good_to_know: Gustave Eiffel's company built the tower between 1887 and 1889 as the centrepiece of the 1889 World's Fair. Parisians nicknamed it "La dame de fer", the Iron Lady. It's 330 metres tall and still the tallest structure in Paris.

card.hook: Twelve avenues crash into one giant arch, and somehow it's the calmest-looking thing in the picture. The trick is to stand back and let the Champs-Élysées do the work.
card.stand_here: Stand about 95 m east of the arch, near Avenue de Friedland (that's where the phone icon is), and face west with the whole arch straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole arch with the avenue leading to it. Go 0.5x for more trees, street and sky, then try 3x for the sculpture and the top of the arch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the middle of the arch up with the centre line, and hold the phone level so the sides stay straight.
card.best_time: Morning to early afternoon usually works best, because the side facing the Champs-Élysées is lit then, and early morning tends to be quieter. In the evening, switch on night mode and keep your arms tucked in to stay steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the median at the first pedestrian crosswalk down from the arch, well away from the roundabout, where the arch fills the background. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low so the arch rises over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement well down the avenue, facing back up toward the arch, while you stand closer to it, so you and the whole arch fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Traffic on the avenue and around the roundabout moves fast, so take care with any photo stop near the road and hold your phone firmly by busy kerbs. Selfie sticks aren't allowed through the monument's security check, and guides disagree on other rules, so check the official site before you go up.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the trees and lamp posts on both sides point at the arch like arrows, then one where you're pretending to hold it up.
card.good_to_know: Napoleon commissioned the arch in 1806 after the victory at Austerlitz, but it wasn't finished until 1836. It's about 49.5 m tall and nearly 45 m wide. Beneath it lies the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier from the First World War, marked by an eternal flame.

card.hook: A giant glass pyramid parked in front of an old stone palace sounds like a mistake, but it makes one of the best photos in Paris. The glass picks up the sky and the palace wings, so every shot comes with a free reflection.
card.stand_here: Stand about 200 m west of the pyramid, at the west end of the Cour Napoléon near the Arc du Carrousel (that's the phone icon on the map). Face east and you'll see the whole pyramid with the palace wings around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the wide view with the palace around the pyramid. Want the glass pattern up close? Walk into the courtyard, switch to zoom 0.5x and tilt up a little.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pyramid, then slide the brightness down a touch to make it a bit darker, so the glass and the sky both keep their detail.
card.best_time: It's the museum's main entrance, so the area around the base may be busy. If you're there after dark, try night mode and rest your phone on a wall or railing, if the pyramid is lit.
card.selfie_here: Head into the Cour Napoléon courtyard in front of the pyramid and stand beside one of the shallow pools, which gives you the reflection. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the glass pyramid and palace over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the west side of the Cour Napoléon near the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel, facing east, while you stand by a shallow pool in front of the pyramid, and ask them to hold the phone low to catch the reflection.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed in the Louvre's permanent collections, and we found no rule for the outdoor courtyard. The paving joints in the Cour Napoléon can be uneven, so watch your step while you walk backwards for the perfect shot.
card.challenge: Find a spot where the glass diamonds run in clean diagonal lines across your whole frame, then see if you can fit one of the three smaller pyramids in too.
card.good_to_know: I. M. Pei designed the Louvre Pyramid, and it was completed in 1989 as part of the Grand Louvre project. It's 21.6 metres tall, with a square base 34 metres along each side. It's made of 673 glass panes (603 rhombus-shaped, 70 triangular).
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 200 m west of the pyramid, at the west end of the Cour Napoléon near the Arc du Carrousel (that's the phone icon on the map). Face east and you'll see the whole pyramid with the palace wings around it.

card.hook: You're about to go underground to meet six million people, but the best warm-up photo is above ground, on a busy square in south Paris. The entrance is easy to miss until you're standing right at it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Place Denfert-Rochereau, where the phone icon on the map sits right at the entrance. It's about 1 minute on foot, to the south-west of Denfert-Rochereau station. Step back a few paces and face the entrance so it fits in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the entrance and the square around it. Try zoom 0.5x to fit in more of the square, but keep the entrance away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched. Use zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for signs and doorways.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the entrance, then drag the brightness slider down a touch if the sky is bright and the doorway looks dark.
card.best_time: Daylight is easiest for the outside shots. Go earlier or later in the day if you want fewer people in your frame.
card.selfie_here: Take it on Place Denfert-Rochereau, in front of the green-glass entrance building, which is a former 1787 toll gate. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and keep the building over your shoulder with a bit of the square showing.
card.ask_someone: Cross to the far side of the road from the Denfert-Rochereau metro exit, where the Catacombs building is the first one you see, and ask a passer-by to photograph you with it in view (this spot is approximate, so shuffle until the whole building fits).
card.rules_and_safety: No flash inside, and don't touch the remains, though photography is allowed. Check the official site for current photo rules and follow any signs. There are many steps and narrow, dark passages, and the site isn't recommended for young children or people with heart problems or anxiety.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the entrance with a bit of the square, then one tight detail, and caption it 'Gate of Hell, but make it a queue.'
card.good_to_know: The Catacombs are an underground ossuary in old limestone quarries beneath the Left Bank, holding the remains of more than six million people. From the late 1780s, remains were carried here by night in covered wagons from overcrowded city cemeteries. It opened to visitors in 1874 and has been a Paris Musées site since 2013. The old city gate here was called the Barrière d'Enfer, the 'Gate of Hell', which makes a great caption.

card.hook: Notre-Dame lost most of its roof and its spire in the April 2019 fire, and you can now photograph it freshly restored. Expect a few thousand new friends in your frame.
card.stand_here: Head to Parvis Notre-Dame and stand at the phone icon, about 110 m north-west of the subject. Face south-east, and if people block your view, shuffle sideways a few steps rather than coming forward.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit both towers and the front in one shot. Go to 0.5x if you move closer or the crowd squeezes you in, and use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the carvings, the rose window and the tower tops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the two towers with the vertical lines so they don't lean.
card.best_time: Mid to late afternoon or early evening is a good bet, when the front catches warmer light. Early morning is usually quieter if you want fewer people in the shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the top of the staircase on the Quai de Montebello, down toward the Notre-Dame Batobus stop, where the trees open up and the cathedral is framed over the Seine. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the cathedral over your shoulder. Square René Viviani, the small garden on the left bank, is a quieter backup.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the Parvis Notre-Dame (Place Jean-Paul II) and ask them to step well back from the cathedral so the whole front fits, while you stand on the square in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Notre-Dame is a working Catholic cathedral, so check the official site before you go for entry arrangements and any rules on dress or photography inside.
card.challenge: Zoom in on the carved doorways and find your favourite stone face, then see if you can get a shot of it with no heads in front.
card.good_to_know: Work on Notre-Dame began in 1163 and was largely finished by 1260. It's one of the finest examples of French Gothic architecture, so look for the flying buttresses, big rose windows and richly carved figures. After the 2019 fire it reopened in December 2024, about three years later. In the early 21st century it drew about 12 million visitors a year, making it the most visited monument in Paris.

card.hook: Sacré-Cœur sits at the very top of Montmartre like a pale, white-domed show-off, and you can spot it from lots of corners of Paris. Lucky for you, it's also one of the easiest big buildings in the city to photograph on a phone.
card.stand_here: Head to Rue du Cardinal Dubois and stand about 50 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face north and keep clear of doorways and paths so you don't block other visitors.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front and the domes in, since you're close. Then try 1x for a tighter facade shot, and 2x or 5x (if your phone has them) for the domes and the carved stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white stonework, then slide the brightness a little darker if the facade looks washed out.
card.best_time: Check how the light falls on the facade and wait for a moment when it looks even. At dusk, switch on night mode and rest your phone against something solid to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Go down to Place Saint-Pierre, by the carousel, at the foot of the hill, where the basilica rises behind you. Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the dome over your shoulder. One guide says selfie sticks crowd the steps by 10am, so earlier is easier.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the foot of the double staircase in Square Louise Michel while you climb the steps, so they can catch you with the basilica behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Sacré-Cœur is a working place of worship, so check the official site for visiting arrangements and dress expectations, and be discreet with your phone near the entrances. One visitor guide recommends Abbesses (Line 12) over Anvers (Line 2) as the safer Métro station.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, line the central dome up with a vertical line so it stands up straight, and sneak a lamp post or some steps into the bottom of the frame.
card.good_to_know: Paul Abadie's design was picked from seventy-seven proposals. Building started in 1875, the church was finished in 1914, and it was consecrated in 1919. The hilltop ground was unstable, so eighty-three deep wells were dug and filled with rock and concrete, and five more architects followed Abadie.

card.hook: Seventeen different materials on one façade: the Palais Garnier is the show-off of Paris, and it knows it. Your only problem is deciding which bit to photograph first.
card.stand_here: Head to Place de l'Opéra and stand about 35 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The whole façade is straight ahead of you, with the square in front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which fits most of the façade. Go 0.5x if you want the whole front and lots of sky. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the gilded figures, the busts and The Dance by Carpeaux.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the middle of the building up with the centre line, then tap the façade and slide it a touch darker so the gold keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Daylight suits it, because the gilded groups at the top catch the light. People and traffic keep crossing the square, so take a few frames and pick the cleanest. If you see it lit after dark, try night mode and brace your phone against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Inside, try the loggias along either side of the Grand Staircase, away from the crowd at the foot of the stairs. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the staircase's baroque curves sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the south end of Avenue de l'Opéra facing north, while you stand near the façade on Place de l'Opéra so the whole building is behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks and monopods are not permitted inside, though sources disagree a little, so leave yours at home. card.hook: From the courtyard, the Sainte-Chapelle looks like a tall, grey stone church. Step inside and the walls turn into coloured glass. It's two very different photos in one stop.
card.stand_here: Stand in the courtyard in front of the Sainte-Chapelle, about 40 m west of the chapel, at the phone icon on the map. Face east and walk back as far as the courtyard allows.
card.zoom: Outside, start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tall building in. Indoors, use 0.5x where space is tight and 1x for a more natural view of the windows. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for single glass panels or carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest bit of coloured glass, then slide it a little darker so the colours stay rich instead of washing out.
card.best_time: For the glass, a bright day usually gives the strongest colour. Outside, soft daylight shows the stonework evenly, and a quieter time of day helps keep crowds out of your shots.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the Upper Chapel and stand with the stained-glass windows behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, so you and a big slice of colour both fit. The exact spot inside is approximate, so just find a place where the windows fill your background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the Palais de Justice courtyard (Boulevard du Palais side) and frame you with the chapel behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed inside, but selfies are fine. The spiral stone staircase up to the Upper Chapel is narrow and winding, so take it slowly. Check the official site for photography rules before you shoot indoors.
card.challenge: Turn your phone to portrait, switch on the gridlines, and get the whole chapel in one shot with its vertical lines dead straight.
card.good_to_know: King Louis IX had the Sainte-Chapelle built between 1238 and 1248 to hold his relics of the Passion, including the Crown of Thorns. It has two levels: the lower one for courtiers, servants and soldiers, and the upper one for the royal family and their guests. The upper windows hold one of the biggest collections of original 13th-century stained glass anywhere.

card.hook: The Musée d'Orsay used to be a railway station, and with those big arches it still looks like it's waiting for a very posh train. Its long stone frontage is a gift to a phone camera.
card.stand_here: Stand about 210 m north-east of the museum, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. That distance gives the whole building room to breathe.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole frontage with the river in front of it. Then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to fill the frame with the building or pick out the big clock faces and arched windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's horizontal edges with them, and keep your phone level so the frontage doesn't lean.
card.best_time: It's a busy place, so take a few frames with the crowds and a few when there's a gap. If the building is lit up in the evening, try night mode and rest your elbows on something steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the middle of the Passerelle Léopold-Sédar-Senghor footbridge, where its two levels meet, with the Orsay riverfront to the south of you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the museum over your shoulder. A photo guide calls the bridge a good vantage point with the Orsay in view, though it isn't officially a selfie spot. For an indoor option, one guide says the big glass clock face (the third one, near the Seine-side corner of the upper floor) frames the river and the Right Bank.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the Pont Royal, across the Seine from the museum's riverfront, and ask a passer-by to frame you with the museum alongside the river.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is not allowed inside the museum, but personal photos of the permanent rooms are. Selfie sticks are reported as banned, though that comes from third-party sites, so check on arrival.
card.challenge: Can you get one of the big clock faces and one arched window into a single shot, without anyone's head photobombing it?
card.good_to_know: The building was the Gare d'Orsay, built between 1898 and 1900 in the Beaux-Arts style, and it opened as a museum in December 1986. It holds the largest collection of Impressionist and post-Impressionist art in the world, with Monet, Renoir, Degas, Cézanne and van Gogh among the names. In the square next to the museum, look out for six bronze sculpture groups originally made for an Exposition Universelle.

card.hook: A giant red windmill on the roof of a building in the middle of a Paris boulevard: it sounds like a joke, but it's the whole point. Even if you only want a quick snap, this is a good one.

card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the centre median of Boulevard de Clichy facing the windmill, while you stand ahead of them so the whole building fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The street in front is busy, so watch the traffic. One guide says the Pigalle area can be a bit sketchy after dark, so stay alert if you're there late. Shows inside are for paying visitors, but you can photograph the outside from the street.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the windmill and the sign together, then one sideways shot with the street in front, and see which one you'd put on a postcard.
card.good_to_know: The Moulin Rouge opened on 6 October 1889 as the Jardin de Paris, an outdoor garden café-concert at the foot of Montmartre hill. The first building burned down in 1915, and the rebuilt venue reopened in 1925. It's best known as the birthplace of the modern can-can, and Toulouse-Lautrec's posters helped make its name famous.

card.hook: Picture a kid in a tiny sailor-style crouch, pushing a model boat across a huge octagonal pond while the palace looks on. That's the Jardin du Luxembourg, and it's a gift for a wide shot with a bit of life in it.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Cour de la Présidence, about 150 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the basin and the long views along the paths. Go to 0.5x for the terraces and sweeping lawns, then 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for statues, boats and fountain details. Don't push the zoom much further, as the detail gets soft.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up a path or the pond edge with one of them, because all those straight lines will show any tilt.
card.best_time: Morning or later in the afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows under the trees. Mornings are also often quieter.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the south edge of the Grand Bassin among the green metal chairs, with the Luxembourg Palace rising behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you want the palace to fit over your shoulder, and add the palm-framed flower bowls for an instantly Parisian backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the southern terrace of the Grand Bassin and shoot north across the pond, while you stand at the pond's southern edge with the Palais du Luxembourg behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Handheld photos for personal use are fine throughout the garden, so selfies and passer-by shots are good to go. Opening times can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a small boat on the water in the middle distance, with the pond edge sitting dead level on a gridline. Bonus points if a statue peeks in at the edge.
card.good_to_know: Marie de' Medici began the garden in 1612, when she built the Luxembourg Palace as her new home. Today it's owned by the French Senate, which meets in the palace. The garden covers 23 hectares, and the Medici Fountain, from 1620, sits in a shadier spot on the eastern side.

card.hook: Place de la Concorde is so wide that one photo can only tell part of the story, and that's the fun of it. You've got a tall obelisk, two fountains, rows of lamps and grand buildings all competing for your attention.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map in Place de la Concorde, about 90 m north-east of the obelisk. Face south-west and the Luxor Obelisk is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the obelisk, fountains and lamps into one big shot. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the top of the obelisk or a statue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the obelisk up with a vertical line so it stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people and less traffic in your shot. Around sunset and dusk, the lamps and fountains look especially good against the sky.
card.selfie_here: Go to the base of the Luxor Obelisk and face the Champs-Élysées, so the obelisk is at your back. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold it a little low, and you'll get the obelisk over your shoulder with the avenue and the Arc de Triomphe in view. One guide says the sunset light works well from this spot.
card.ask_someone: For a shot with the whole square behind you, try one of the two elevated terraces of the Tuileries Garden, which overlook everything, and ask a passer-by to take it.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is a major traffic roundabout and the obelisk stands on a traffic island, so take extreme care and cross only at the marked crossings.
card.challenge: Collect the set of three: one wide shot of the whole square, one of the obelisk against the sky, and one of a fountain or a statue.
card.good_to_know: At 7.6 hectares, this is the largest square in Paris. The Luxor Obelisk, a gift from Egypt, was raised here in October 1836 in front of a big crowd. The square was renamed Concorde in 1795 as a gesture of reconciliation.

card.hook: Picture a straight alley with trees lined up on both sides like they're queuing politely, and every line in the picture pointing the same way. That's the Tuileries, and it's why your photo will look good almost without trying.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the alley and the trees. Go to 0.5x if you want the full width of the garden and lots of sky, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a statue or someone strolling in the distance.

It covers 25.5 hectares, and it hosted the Olympic and Paralympic cauldron during the 2024 Games.

card.challenge: Pick one small section of the dome, zoom in until it fills the screen, and see if you can get it with perfectly straight lines and no stray shoppers at the edges.
card.good_to_know: The dome is a landmark of the Galeries Lafayette department store at 40 Boulevard Haussmann, in the 9th arrondissement. It makes a good phone subject because it's a strong, simple shape with lots of detail to look at. You can grab a quick shot on the way past or spend a few minutes on a careful frame.

card.hook: The Grand Palais is about 200 m long, so if you stand too close, your phone loses the argument. Back up, take a breath, and pick what you want: the whole front, a detail, or the sweep of the roofline.

card.good_to_know: The Palais de Chaillot was built for the 1937 International Exhibition. In 1948 the United Nations General Assembly met here and adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and a stone on the esplanade marks the event.

card.hook: Picture a 196-metre-wide façade with a huge Dôme sitting dead centre, like the building was designed for your phone screen. It was built for veterans of Louis XIV's wars, but the symmetry works for you too.

Today it holds the army museum and Napoleon's tomb, and it still has a retirement home for former soldiers. The Dôme rises 107 metres, making it the tallest church building in Paris and taller than Notre Dame.

card.hook: Picture a gallery that forgot to hide its insides: pipes, steel and tubes are all out on the front, painted like a giant toy machine. Yes, that's the Centre Pompidou, and it's very hard to take a boring photo of it.

card.good_to_know: The Centre Pompidou opened on 31 January 1977, and its design was chosen from 681 competition entries. The colours are a code: green for plumbing, blue for climate control, yellow for electrics and red for circulation and safety equipment. Inside are a large public library and the Musée National d'Art Moderne, the largest museum of modern art in Europe.

card.good_to_know: The Panthéon began as a church. Louis XV wanted a grander home for the relics of Saint Genevieve, Paris's patron saint, and architect Jacques-Germain Soufflot designed it. Building ran from 1758 to 1790, and neither man lived to see it finished. By then the Revolution had begun, so it became a mausoleum for France's distinguished citizens. It stands about 83 metres high, and the dome you see from outside is the outermost of three set inside one another.
